result: Loss of Ntn1 causes DRG axons to escape from the dorsal funiculus at the time of bifurcation. Wholemount staining with tissue clearing revealed misprojecting fibers that appear in the hindlimb region where the dorsal funiculus starts to emerge, with quantification showing an average of 22 fibers per DRG proximal to the DREZ, decreasing to 14 fibers/DRG distally. Genetic labeling confirmed these misprojections originate from DRG neurons.
evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C31-C37 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (wholemount staining, tissue clearing, genetic labeling, transverse sections) demonstrating that Ntn1 loss causes DRG axon misprojections at the time of bifurcation. The quantitative data (C33) and temporal analysis (C35-C36) strengthen the conclusion. The genetic labeling (C6) definitively establishes the DRG origin of misprojections.

result: Genetic labeling using Neurog1-CreERT2 and tdTomato reporter confirms that misprojecting axons in Ntn1 mutants originate from DRG neurons. Co-labeling analysis shows that all tdTomato-labeled misprojections are NF-positive and come directly from the DREZ, while D2 interneurons do not contribute to NF-labeled misprojections.
evaluation: Claims C38-C47 provide strong evidence through genetic lineage tracing that misprojections originate from DRG neurons. The co-labeling analysis (C41-C42) and exclusion of D2 interneurons (C44-C45) strengthen the conclusion. The authors appropriately acknowledge potential underrepresentation due to incomplete Cre activity (C46), demonstrating scientific rigor.

result: Sparse labeling analysis reveals that in Ntn1 mutants, approximately 55% of bifurcated and 70% of non-bifurcated axons misprojected outside the defined dorsal funiculus, compared to nearly all axons staying within the DREZ in wild-type animals. This demonstrates that loss of Ntn1 alters DRG axon guidance at the DREZ during bifurcation.
evaluation: Claims C48-C50 provide quantitative single-axon analysis demonstrating the guidance defect in Ntn1 mutants. The comparison between WT (n=11/12 bifurcated, n=14/14 non-bifurcated staying in DREZ) and mutants (~55% and ~70% misprojecting) provides clear statistical evidence. The conclusion (C50) is well-supported by the data.

result: Triple mutants lacking Ntn1, Slit1, and Slit2 show complete disorganization of the dorsal funiculus with distinct phenotypes compared to single or double mutants. Slit1/Slit2 mutants show straight horizontal misprojections entering the spinal cord, while Ntn1 mutants show wavy dorsal misprojections along the pial surface. Triple mutants exhibit both types of misprojections with additive defects, demonstrating different guidance roles for these pathways.
evaluation: Claims C54-C74 provide comprehensive comparative analysis of single, double, and triple mutants using multiple imaging approaches (lateral, dorsal, transverse views) with quantitative measurements. The distinct trajectories (straight vs. wavy, horizontal vs. dorsal) and additive phenotypes in triple mutants strongly support independent guidance roles. The quantitative data (C62, C66, C69) strengthens the conclusions.

result: DiI labeling analysis at E12.5 shows that bifurcation is preserved in Ntn1, Slit1/Slit2, and triple mutants, with 26/27 WT axons, 32/34 Ntn1 mutant axons, 28/29 Slit1/Slit2 mutant axons, and 20/21 triple mutant axons forming two branches. This demonstrates that neither Ntn1 nor Slit is required for branch formation itself.
evaluation: Claims C75-C80 provide clear quantitative evidence from single-axon DiI labeling that bifurcation rates are similar across all genotypes (>90% in all cases). The conclusion (C80) that neither pathway is required for branch formation is well-supported by the data. This is an important negative result that distinguishes guidance from branching.

result: Quantitative analysis of bifurcation angles reveals that while average angles remain similar across genotypes (115.4° WT, 118.9° Slit mutants, 108.0° Ntn1 mutants, 110.7° triple mutants), angle deviation and difference between branches increase progressively. Triple mutants show the most severe defects with 37.8° deviation and 74.6° angle difference, demonstrating additive roles of Ntn1 and Slit in guiding the two branches.
evaluation: Claims C81-C87 provide rigorous quantitative analysis of bifurcation geometry. The preservation of average angles but increased deviation and difference metrics effectively captures the guidance defects. The additive phenotype in triple mutants (C85-C86) with significantly increased deviation (37.8°) and difference (74.6°) compared to single mutants provides strong evidence for independent guidance roles.

result: Analysis of receptor mutants (DCC and Robo1/Robo2) shows phenotypes similar to ligand mutants. DCC mutants exhibit dorsal misprojections similar to Ntn1 mutants, Robo1/Robo2 mutants show horizontal misprojections similar to Slit mutants, and triple receptor mutants show both types of misprojections with additive defects. This demonstrates that loss of either ligand or receptor has the same impact on DRG axon guidance.
evaluation: Claims C88-C99 provide strong genetic evidence that the phenotypes are mediated through the cognate receptors. The parallel phenotypes between ligand and receptor mutants (C91, C94-C96) and quantitative analysis showing additive defects in triple receptor mutants (C97-C98) support the conclusion that these are bona fide signaling pathways. The consistency strengthens the overall model.

result: The study demonstrates that development of T-shaped DRG bifurcation requires both Ntn1 and Slit signaling, which regulate different aspects of guidance. Loss of both pathways results in complete disorganization of the dorsal funiculus with nearly all DRG axons leaving the DREZ. The distinct trajectories (horizontal for Slit loss, dorsal for Ntn1 loss) and additive defects demonstrate non-redundant, multi-factorial guidance mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C100-C125 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model. The evidence from multiple mutant combinations, distinct phenotypes, and additive defects strongly supports the conclusion of multi-factorial guidance. The claim of first report of such severe defect (C118) is appropriately qualified. The comparative analysis (C119-C122) effectively distinguishes the two pathways.

result: Loss of Ntn1 leads to guidance errors at the time of bifurcation (E10.5), with misprojecting axons growing dorsally along the pial surface rather than stopping at the DREZ. Single axon analysis rules out a requirement for bifurcation itself, as most axons still form two branches. The similar defect in DCC mutants supports a guidance function for Ntn1 signaling at the time of bifurcation.
evaluation: Claims C102-C109 effectively synthesize the temporal and mechanistic aspects of Ntn1 function. The timing (E10.5), trajectory (dorsal/pial), and preservation of bifurcation (C105) are all well-supported by data. The comparison to zebrafish DCC function (C109) provides useful context. The conclusion that Ntn1 functions in guidance rather than bifurcation per se is well-justified.

result: The authors propose a model where Slit guides the primary axon to turn into the DREZ, CNP stimulates second branch formation, and Ntn1 regulates the trajectory of both branches as they grow along the DREZ. This demonstrates that formation of T-shaped bifurcation requires multiple molecular mechanisms for both branch formation and guidance.
evaluation: Claims C126-C127, C132 present a working model integrating the current findings with previous work on CNP. The model is well-supported by the distinct phenotypes and temporal sequence of events. However, the sequential model (C126) involves some inference beyond the direct data, as the experiments don't directly test the temporal sequence. The overall conclusion (C127) about multiple mechanisms is strongly supported.

result: Two potential mechanisms are proposed for Ntn1 function: (1) a permissive/adhesive function through DCC that encourages growth while restricting trajectory within the DREZ, or (2) a repulsive function mediated by DCC and/or Unc5C receptors, supported by Unc5C expression in DRG neurons and in vitro repulsive activity.
evaluation: Claims C110-C114 present speculative mechanisms (C110, C112 explicitly marked as speculation). While the expression data (C113) and in vitro data (C114) are cited, the current study does not distinguish between these mechanisms. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities requiring future investigation. More direct functional tests would be needed to support either mechanism.

result: The authors propose that the DREZ is an evolving structure constructed at the location where DRG axons bifurcate through interactions with dorsal spinal cord cells, rather than being defined by preexisting cell types. This is supported by zebrafish studies showing growth cone interactions with the glial environment and DCC control of invadopodia stabilization.
evaluation: Claims C128-C129 present a conceptual framework that is partially speculative (marked as inference/speculation). While the zebrafish data (C130-C131) from cited studies provides support, the current study in mouse does not directly test this model. The perspective is reasonable but represents interpretation rather than direct demonstration. The conclusion (C132) about the importance of both branching and guidance is better supported.

result: The authors discuss potential roles for boundary cap cells and dorsal interneurons in DREZ formation. Boundary cap cells are associated with the dorsal root entry site starting at E12 in rat and could potentially shape the DREZ. Dorsal interneurons show migration defects in Ntn1/DCC mutants and could produce guidance factors, as loss of TAG-1/Axonin-1 causes similar DREZ defects.
evaluation: Claims C133-C140 discuss potential cellular mechanisms but are largely speculative (C135, C137, C139 explicitly marked as speculation). The cited evidence for boundary cap cells (C134, C136) and interneuron defects (C138, C140) comes from other studies. The current work does not directly test these mechanisms. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future investigation but are not demonstrated by the current data.

result: The manuscript establishes background knowledge about DRG axon development, including the anatomy and function of the dorsal funiculus, the timing and location of bifurcation at the DREZ, the role of CNP/Npr2 in branch formation, and previous findings on Slit/Robo signaling showing incomplete penetrance affecting ~50% of DRG axons.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C12-C22 establish the background context through citations to previous literature. These are appropriately cited established facts about DRG anatomy, development, and previous genetic studies. The claims accurately represent prior knowledge and set up the rationale for the current study. This background is essential for understanding the significance of the new findings.

result: Ntn1 is expressed in the spinal cord including the floor plate, ventricular zone, and lateral domain in the dorsal horn from E10.5 to E11.5. Previous studies identified aberrant sensory axon entry at E11.5-E12.5 and suggested Ntn1 prevents premature ingrowth via repulsion. Ntn1 proteins are made by ventricular zone progenitors and deposited along the pial layer adjacent to the DREZ.
evaluation: Claims C23-C28 establish Ntn1 expression patterns through in situ hybridization (C27) consistent with previous studies (C23-C26, C28). The expression data (Figure 1 supplement 1A-B) supports the localization claims. The summary of previous interpretations (C24-C26) is accurate and sets up the contrast with the current findings. This provides essential context for understanding the new guidance role identified.

result: In wild-type embryos, DRG axons extend dorsally, enter the spinal cord, and form the dorsal funiculus running along the rostrocaudal axis. The dorsal funiculus is thicker near the forelimb than hindlimb due to developmental delay along the rostrocaudal axis.
evaluation: Claims C29-C30 describe normal DRG axon development in WT embryos based on wholemount immunostaining (Figure 1A, C). The observation about differential thickness (C30) is a reasonable inference from developmental timing and is supported by the images. This establishes the baseline for comparison with mutants.

result: Previous work showed Slit signaling is required for proper guidance during bifurcation but does not affect all DRG axons. The current study hypothesizes that Ntn1 and Slit have different guidance functions based on the observation that Ntn1 mutant misprojections appear on the dorsal pial surface outside the spinal cord, unlike Slit mutant phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C51-C53 establish the rationale for investigating Ntn1 by contrasting with previous Slit findings. The hypothesis (C53) is reasonable based on the distinct phenotypes observed. Claims C3-C4 and C51 accurately cite previous work. Claim C52 is supported by the transverse section data. The hypothesis is appropriately tested in subsequent experiments.
